broad.question: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

hypotheses.label: C4

source_paper.title: An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide.

hypotheses.builds_on: The finding from the paper that a CrTaO4-based oxide forms and contributes to the oxidation resistance of NV1, with non-stoichiometry being an important factor.
hypotheses.what_is_new: Proposes specifically tuning the alloy’s Ta content to optimize the formation of a non-stoichiometric CrTaO4, thus providing a self-healing mechanism not directly explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Increasing the refractory element Ta content will promote formation of a non‐stoichiometric CrTaO4 phase that more effectively accommodates excess Al and Cr, thereby creating a denser, self‐healing oxide scale that limits oxygen ingress at high temperatures.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A typical high-entropy refractory alloy containing Al, Cr, Mo, Nb, Si, Ta, Ti, such as the NV1 alloy with its as-cast dendritic microstructure and element segregation.
hypothesis.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by increasing the Ta content (e.g., by ~10% relative to the baseline) while keeping other elements constant.
hypothesis.conditions: Isothermal oxidation tests at high temperatures (e.g., 1100 °C) for durations of 100–200 hours in air.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The formation and stability of a non-stoichiometric CrTaO4-based oxide that forms a continuous, low-porosity scale.
hypothesis.mechanism: Enhanced Ta availability promotes the formation of a CrTaO4 phase with altered lattice parameters that can incorporate additional Al and Cr. This modification suppresses the formation of discrete, less-protective oxides (e.g. Al2O3 or Cr2O3) and minimizes porosity by balancing cation diffusion. The denser oxide reduces both outward diffusion of reactive species and inward oxygen diffusion, yielding superior oxidation resistance.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Ta-enhanced alloy is expected to show lower mass gains (smaller oxidation weight gain) and a more uniform and denser surface oxide layer under identical high-temperature exposure conditions.
hypothesis.baseline: The original NV1 alloy as described in PMC6513993, which forms a primarily CrTaO4-based oxide layer that becomes denser at 1100 °C but has some porosity and heterogeneous features.
hypothesis.boundary: Works in high-temperature regimes (around 1100 °C) and long-term exposures (≥100 hours), but may not be effective under very rapid cycling or at much lower temperatures where diffusion kinetics are significantly diminished.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance and the optimum Ta content require experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one with the baseline composition and one with increased Ta content. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation at 1100 °C for up to 200 hours under identical conditions.
measurements: Thermogravimetric measurements (mass gain curves) over time.
Surface and cross-sectional microstructure analysis (SEM/EDS) to assess oxide scale density and continuity.
Phase identification via XRD to check for non-stoichiometric CrTaO4 formation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ta-enhanced alloy does not exhibit a significantly lower oxidation weight gain and the oxide scale does not demonstrate increased density and continuity compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C10

source_paper.title: The Effect of Fe Addition in the RM(Nb)IC Alloy Nb-30Ti-10Si-2Al-5Cr-3Fe-5Sn-2Hf (at.%) on Its Microstructure, Complex Concentrated and High Entropy Phases, Pest Oxidation, Strength and Contamination with Oxygen, and a Comparison with Other RM(Nb)ICs, Refractory Complex Concentrated Alloys (RCCAs) and Refractory High Entropy Alloys (RHEAs).

hypotheses.builds_on: the established role of reactive elements in enhancing oxide scale adhesion in superalloys and stainless steels.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies the concept of reactive element effects—commonly used in conventional high-temperature alloys—to high-entropy alloys, providing a novel route for improving oxidation resistance via microstructural modification at the oxide scale interface.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Minor additions of a reactive element such as yttrium (Y) to high‐entropy alloys will improve the adhesion and stability of the protective oxide layer by modifying grain boundary characteristics in the oxide scale.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A baseline HEA similar to those studied in refractory systems that, when oxidized, develop a scale (e.g., with Sn-rich A15 features) that may suffer from spallation due to insufficient adhesion.
hypothesis.intervention: Incorporate a trace amount (approximately 0.2 at.%) of yttrium into the HEA composition while keeping the major alloying elements constant.
hypothesis.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in air at around 800 °C for a duration of 100 h.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A protective oxide scale enriched in yttrium at grain boundaries, leading to reduced void formation and improved interfacial adhesion between the oxide and the underlying substrate.
hypothesis.mechanism: Yttrium, a well-known reactive element in oxidation-resistant alloys, segregates to oxide grain boundaries and interfaces, lowering the surface energy and promoting stronger bonds between oxide grains. This leads to a more continuous, adherent oxide scale with improved resistance to mechanical disruption and spallation. The enhanced adhesion slows down oxygen transport into the substrate, thereby improving the alloy's oxidation resistance.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Y-modified HEA should show a reduced oxide spallation rate, lower mass gain during oxidation, and a more uniformly adherent, crack-free oxide scale. Microstructural analyses would reveal Y enrichment at the oxide’s grain boundaries.
hypothesis.baseline: The HEA without any reactive element addition, which displays a protective oxide layer that is more prone to spalling and non-uniform growth.
hypothesis.boundary: The reactive element mechanism is expected to be effective in high-temperature oxidizing environments (≈700–900 °C) and with very low Y additions that do not alter the overall alloy phase stability.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact optimal concentration of yttrium for maximum improvement without affecting the HEA’s desirable mechanical properties is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one baseline HEA and one with 0.2 at.% Y added. Oxidize both sets at 800 °C for 100 h. Assess the oxide scale adhesion and microstructural characteristics using SEM/EPMA, and measure oxidation mass gain.
measurements: Mass gain kinetics
Microscopic evaluation of oxide scale morphology and spallation events
Chemical mapping to detect Y segregation at the oxide scale grain boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Y does not result in improved oxide adhesion (i.e., similar or increased spallation and no evident Y enrichment at critical interfaces) or if the oxidation mass gain is not significantly lower than that of the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C11

source_paper.title: Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior of Dual-Phase High Entropy Alloy for Concentrating Solar Power Systems.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s identification of phase-specific work function differences and associated micro-galvanic corrosion effects which imply that the noble FCC (L12) phase is more resistant to oxidation.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis explores the role of engineered microstructure—specifically altering the FCC/BCC phase balance—as a mechanistic pathway to achieve improved oxidation resistance through a more continuous protective scale, an approach not directly reported in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A higher volume fraction of the more noble FCC (L12) phase in dual-phase high-entropy alloys governs the development of a continuous and adherent protective oxide scale.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy comprising a dual-phase microstructure with both FCC (L12) and BCC (B2) phases in its as-cast state.
hypothesis.intervention: Process the alloy (via controlled heat treatment or minor composition adjustment) to increase the relative volume fraction of the FCC (L12) phase without altering the overall elemental composition significantly.
hypothesis.conditions: High-temperature oxidation tests in air at 650–750 °C, where diffusion-controlled oxidation and microstructural stability are critical, performed on samples with modified microstructural phase fractions versus a baseline alloy.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The connectivity and continuity of the FCC phase which forms a more noble and oxidation-resistant barrier, compared to the more reactive BCC phase that acts as a micro-anodic site.
hypothesis.mechanism: During oxidation, the noble FCC (L12) phase preferentially forms a stable oxide layer owing to its higher work function, while the reactive BCC (B2) phase tends to dissolve or form nonprotective oxides. Increasing the FCC phase fraction reduces the local galvanic coupling effects that otherwise accelerate oxidation at phase boundaries. This shift provides a more coherent and continuous oxide scale that protects the underlying metal.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Alloys with a higher FCC volume fraction are expected to display a lower oxidation rate (e.g., reduced weight gain and scale spallation) and a more uniform oxide layer, as evidenced by microstructural and compositional analyses (optical/SEM imaging, EBSD mapping) relative to the baseline alloy.
hypothesis.baseline: The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with an original FCC:BCC ratio (e.g., ~77:23 as reported in the paper).
hypothesis.boundary: Applicable under high-temperature oxidation environments (650–750 °C) where the stability of the dual-phase microstructure is maintained; may not extend to conditions where phase transformations dominate.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The critical FCC volume fraction threshold for optimum oxidation protection is not known precisely and may depend on other simultaneous microstructural variables.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one processed to have an increased FCC phase fraction (e.g., via a tailored heat-treatment schedule) and one baseline sample with the original phase fraction. Expose both to identical high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., air at 700 °C for 50 hours), then compare oxide layer uniformity, spallation tendency, and overall oxidation rate via weight gain and microstructural characterizations.
measurements: Phase fraction analysis (using EBSD)
Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (via SEM/XRD)
Weight gain measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with increased FCC phase fraction does not demonstrate a lower oxidation rate and improved oxide scale continuity compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C12

source_paper.title: Initial Oxidation Behavior of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Coating Produced by Atmospheric Plasma Spraying in the Range of 650 °C to 1000 °C.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s findings on the role of Al diffusion and oxide scale formation [PMC10856430::web::014::4_discussions] combined with passivation principles from established oxidation literature [TXT::Passivation_(chemistry)::004].
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes an in-situ powder modification step—co-depositing nano-scale Al2O3 particles—to actively seed and control oxide formation, a strategy not explored in the original paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Incorporation of Nano‐Scale Al2O3 Seed Particles in the Feedstock to Nucleate and Stabilize the Protective Oxide Layer
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A conventional plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating that develops a mixed oxide layer with internal Al depletion during high-temperature exposure.
hypothesis.intervention: Modify the powder feedstock by pre-mixing or dispersing a low volume fraction (<5 vol.%) of nano-scale Al2O3 particles to be co-deposited during plasma spraying.
hypothesis.conditions: Expose both the nano-seeded and conventional HEA coatings to isothermal oxidation in air at 900–1000°C for 100 hours.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The pre-dispersed nano-Al2O3 particles will act as heterogeneous nucleation sites for forming a continuous and adherent Al2O3 scale at the very early stages of oxidation.
hypothesis.mechanism: The nano-Al2O3 seeds lower the energy barrier for homogeneous nucleation of Al2O3 by providing substrates with matching crystallographic features, thereby facilitating the formation of a uniform, thin oxide layer. This seed layer then limits uncontrolled Al diffusion (which, in unseeded coatings, often leads to thick, poorly adherent scales due to rapid Al depletion) in accordance with passivation principles [TXT::Passivation_(chemistry)::004]. Additionally, a uniformly distributed seed layer can help maintain the Pilling–Bedworth ratio within the optimum range (1 < RPB < 2) [TXT::Pilling–Bedworth_ratio::002].
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The nano-seeded coatings will display a thinner, more continuous, and adherent Al2O3 layer with reduced internal Al depletion compared to the unmodified HEA. Improvements may include lower scale growth rates and fewer spallation events.
hypothesis.baseline: Standard plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi coatings without nano-scale oxide seeding which develop a mixed and often thicker oxide layer with noticeable Al depletion zones.
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective in oxidation environments at high temperatures (900–1000°C) where Al mobility is significant; at lower temperatures the benefits may be less pronounced.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise dispersion uniformity and optimal nano-Al2O3 content require calibration; the impact on bulk mechanical integrity is not fully predictable.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings: one using the conventional plasma spraying process and one with feedstock modified by a controlled nano-scale Al2O3 dispersion. Oxidize both sets at 900–1000°C for 100 hours in air. Perform cross-sectional SEM/EDS and XRD to examine oxide scale morphology, continuity, thickness, and measure Al concentration profiles.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (via cross-sectional SEM)
Adhesion and integrity of the oxide layer (e.g., via scratch or thermal-cycling tests)
Elemental mapping of Al depletion in the underlying coating (via EDS line scans)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nano-seeded coatings do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in oxide uniformity, reduced scale thickness, and lower internal Al depletion compared to the conventional coatings, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C2

source_paper.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s discussion of interfacial processes and diffusion-limited oxidation kinetics, applying these principles to introduce a reactive dopant that could locally modify the protective scale formation.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis uniquely leverages Hf’s chemical and diffusion characteristics—as opposed to standard dopants like Y—to tailor interfacial properties in HEAs, providing a novel microalloying strategy to enhance oxidation resistance beyond what was explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Minor Hafnium (Hf) Doping Promotes Interfacial Segregation Leading to a Stabilized, Protective Oxide Scale
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy produced via arc melting, homogenization, cold rolling, and recrystallization with a uniform elemental distribution.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce a minor amount (e.g., ~0.5–1 at.%) of Hf by substituting a small fraction of one of the alloying elements (such as Mn or Fe), ensuring overall phase stability.
hypothesis.conditions: Oxidize both the Hf-doped alloy and an undoped control alloy at 400 °C in 10 mbar O₂ for 120 minutes under identical conditions.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The segregation of Hf atoms at the metal/oxide interface, forming localized Hf-rich clusters.
hypothesis.mechanism: Hafnium possesses a high oxygen affinity and a low diffusivity relative to other alloying elements. Under oxidation conditions, Hf tends to segregate at the metal/oxide interface where it forms stable oxides or clusters that act as pinning centers to reduce the mobility of cations and inhibit further growth of the oxide scale. This slowed cation diffusion results in a thinner, more adherent and coherent protective scale. The approach builds on the paper’s insights regarding interfacial diffusion and element-specific oxidation kinetics, while leveraging Hf’s unique properties known in high-temperature alloy literature.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The Hf-doped samples will display oxide scales with a reduced overall thickness, enhanced uniformity, and improved adherence compared to undoped samples. Hf enrichment at the oxide/metal interface should be observable via atom probe tomography (APT) or high-resolution STEM-EDS.
hypothesis.baseline: Undoped HEA samples that form the layered oxide structure with typical compositional gradients and some scale defects, as described in the paper.
hypothesis.boundary: Effective under moderate oxidation conditions (around 400 °C and 10 mbar O₂) where Hf can segregate without causing bulk phase instability; the optimal Hf concentration and its segregation kinetics may vary.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact Hf content needed and the quantitative impact on the diffusion barriers at the interface are not precisely predicted.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples, one with ~0.5–1 at.% Hf doping and one undoped. Subject both to oxidation at 400 °C in 10 mbar O₂ for 120 minutes.
measurements: Perform APT or high-resolution STEM-EDS to detect Hf segregation at the oxide/metal interface.
Conduct cross-sectional TEM to compare oxide scale thickness and structure.
Carry out adhesion or spallation tests to assess the mechanical integrity of the oxide scale.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in oxide scale continuity, reduced growth, and clear Hf enrichment at the interface compared to the undoped alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C3

source_paper.title: Oxidation Behavior of Refractory AlNbTiVZr0.25 High-Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s insight into two-stage oxidation kinetics and the detrimental effects of volatile V2O5 formation on scale integrity.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It introduces a pre-oxidation strategy to tailor the oxide scale formation kinetics, aiming to inhibit the formation of volatile and porous oxides and thereby enhance protective behavior, a condition not explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: The oxidation resistance of high-entropy alloys is controlled by a two-stage oxide formation mechanism where a controlled pre-oxidation treatment suppresses the rapid evaporation of volatile V-rich oxides and mediates the nucleation of a coherent, protective mixed oxide scale.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with the composition and microstructure similar to AlNbTiVZr0.25, which typically exhibits a fast transition from slow oxidation to breakaway oxidation due to V2O5 evaporation.
hypothesis.intervention: Implement a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment at a lower temperature (e.g., ~550 °C) for several hours prior to high-temperature oxidation.
hypothesis.conditions: Initial pre-oxidation in air at ~550 °C for 5 hours, followed by standard oxidation testing at 800 °C for 100 hours.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A thin, uniform mixed oxide layer (comprising phases like TiNb2O7 and AlNbO4) that forms during pre-oxidation and acts as a cohesive barrier.
hypothesis.mechanism: By pre-forming a continuous oxide film under conditions that do not trigger significant V-rich oxide evaporation, the subsequent high-temperature oxidation can proceed with reduced volatility-induced porosity and cracking. This pre-oxidized film suppresses rapid oxygen ingress and helps avert the breakaway oxidation seen in untreated samples.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The pre-oxidized alloy should demonstrate a lower mass gain, more uniform and less porous oxide scales, and delayed or suppressed onset of breakaway oxidation as compared to the untreated baseline.
hypothesis.baseline: Direct oxidation at 800 °C of the alloy (without pre-oxidation) that exhibits two-stage kinetics with an early formation of V-rich volatile oxides leading to rapid scale degradation.
hypothesis.boundary: Applicable for high-temperature oxidation where the pre-oxidation temperature is carefully selected to avoid V2O5 evaporation; likely effective in the 700–900 °C regime.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The optimal pre-oxidation time and temperature need to be calibrated, and the interplay with other oxide phases may introduce quantitative uncertainties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of specimens from the same alloy; one group receives a pre-oxidation treatment at 550 °C for 5 hours and the other does not. Subject both sets to oxidation at 800 °C for 100 hours and compare oxidation kinetics, oxide scale morphology (using SEM), and oxide phase composition (using XRD).
measurements: Mass gain curves
XRD phase analysis
SEM imaging for porosity and scale homogeneity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized group does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation rate and improved oxide scale coherence relative to the baseline group, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C5

source_paper.title: An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s observation of heterogeneous oxidation linked to the as-cast dendritic structure and element segregation.
hypotheses.what_is_new: Introduces a microstructural processing route (homogenization) to directly target diffusion uniformity as a means to enhance the protective oxide formation, an approach not explored in the referenced work.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Homogenizing the microstructure by reducing elemental segregation will enable the formation of a more uniform and continuous protective CrTaO4-based oxide scale that limits localized oxidation at high temperatures.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: The as-cast high-entropy alloy with a dendritic microstructure having Mo-rich cores and Cr-/Al-rich interdendritic regions leading to heterogeneous oxidation behavior.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a homogenization heat treatment (or mechanical alloying followed by annealing) to eliminate or reduce chemical segregation and produce a uniformly distributed multi-element solid solution.
hypothesis.conditions: Post-treatment oxidation experiments under isothermal conditions, e.g., 1100 °C for 100–200 hours in air.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A homogenized microstructure that promotes uniform cation diffusion towards the surface, leading to the continuous nucleation and growth of the CrTaO4-based protective oxide layer.
hypothesis.mechanism: A more chemically uniform alloy will reduce preferential paths for oxygen ingress that occur due to local compositional variations. With an evenly distributed supply of Cr, Ta, and Al, the oxide scale will develop consistently over the entire surface, reducing porosity and defects that could compromise the protective effect.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to a cast, segregated microstructure, the homogenized alloy should yield a lower oxidation weight gain and present a denser, evenly distributed oxide layer, as seen in cross-sectional micrographs and EDS mapping.
hypothesis.baseline: The as-cast NV1 alloy, which shows dendritic segregation leading to heterogeneous oxidation behaviors and localized porosity in the oxide scale.
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism is expected to manifest in alloys where the diffusion of key elements is sufficient at high temperatures (≈1100 °C) over long-term exposures; processing parameters must be optimized so that homogenization does not induce excessive grain growth or other deleterious effects.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The extent of improvement and the optimal homogenization parameters may vary depending on the alloy system and are subject to experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one in the as-cast state and one subjected to a homogenization heat treatment. Oxidize both groups under identical conditions (e.g., 1100 °C for 200 hours in air) and compare the resulting oxide scale morphology and mass gain.
measurements: TGA for oxidation kinetics.
SEM/EDS cross-sectional analysis for oxide layer uniformity and porosity.
XRD for phase identification of the surface oxides.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the homogenized samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation mass gain and/or do not exhibit a more continuous and less porous oxide scale compared to the as-cast samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C6

source_paper.title: Microstructure and Composition Evolution of a Fused Slurry Silicide Coating on MoNbTaTiW Refractory High-Entropy Alloy in High-Temperature Oxidation Environment.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s finding that silicon diffusion from a silicide coating leads to protective oxide formation on MoNbTaTiW RHEA.
hypotheses.what_is_new: Instead of applying an external silicide coating, this approach modifies the surface composition of the HEA itself to promote self-passivation via in situ disilicide formation and subsequent oxidation.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Enhancing near‐surface silicon enrichment in a refractory HEA promotes the in situ formation of a disilicide layer that, upon oxidation, converts to a stable SiO2 protective scale.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A baseline MoNbTaTiW high‐entropy alloy with equimolar composition and standard surface conditions.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a laser surface alloying or ion‐implantation process to enrich the near-surface region with additional silicon without altering the bulk composition.
hypothesis.conditions: Expose both the silicon-enriched and baseline HEA samples to the same high-temperature oxidation environment (e.g., at 1000–1300 °C in air for a fixed duration).
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Formation of a disilicide (MSi2) layer near the surface that subsequently oxidizes to form a continuous SiO2 layer.
hypothesis.mechanism: The high local silicon content lowers the Gibbs free energy for disilicide formation, leading to the preferential formation of a nearly stoichiometric MSi2 phase that transforms into a dense, coherent SiO2 scale. The SiO2, with a favorable Pilling–Bedworth ratio (between 1 and 2), acts as a robust diffusion barrier to oxygen ingress, thereby providing oxidation resistance. This builds on the mechanism observed for the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating on MoNbTaTiW, where silicon diffusion played a key role in oxide layer formation (PMC7475834::web::000).
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The silicon-enriched HEA will develop a thicker, more adherent and protective SiO2 scale compared to the baseline alloy; oxidation kinetics will be slower, with reduced oxide spallation and a lower mass gain over the test duration.
hypothesis.baseline: The untreated MoNbTaTiW alloy, which forms a less controlled oxide scale with possible discontinuities and microcracking.
hypothesis.boundary: The effectiveness of the mechanism is expected in high-temperature oxidation environments (around 1000–1300 °C) and where silicon diffusion is not excessively offset by competing reactions. Extreme temperatures causing rapid diffusion of other species may obscure the benefit.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvement and the optimal silicon enrichment level are uncertain without further diffusion and thermodynamic analyses.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of MoNbTaTiW HEA samples—one subjected to laser surface alloying to enrich near-surface silicon and a control group without treatment. Expose both groups to identical high-temperature oxidation tests under static air at 1000 °C and 1300 °C for 1 hour each.
measurements: Mass gain measurement
Cross-sectional SEM/EDS analysis to determine oxide layer thickness and composition
Adhesion tests on the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the silicon-enriched samples do not show statistically significant improvement in forming a uniform, adherent, and thicker SiO2 scale (as evidenced by similar or greater mass gain, oxide spallation, or microcracking compared to the control), the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C7

source_paper.title: High Temperature Oxidation Behavior of an Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co High-Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s observations that the Cr-Mn-Fe-Co HEA forms a mixed oxide layer with spallation issues at higher temperatures (PMC8346963::web::010) and the principle from background on how Al forms protective oxides (TXT::wikipedia::Stainless_steel::028).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes tailoring the composition of HEAs through minor Al additions to deliberately form a stable alumina scale, a strategy not explored in the paper, with a mechanistic basis in controlled oxide thermodynamics and adhesion.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Incorporating a small fraction of aluminum into the high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, slow-growing Al2O3 scale that enhances oxidation resistance by providing an optimal Pilling–Bedworth ratio and improved adhesion compared to the original oxide mixture.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy (HEA) of equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co with a single FCC phase as produced by techniques such as 3D laser printing.
hypothesis.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding 3–5 at.% aluminum while slightly reducing one or more elements to maintain phase stability.
hypothesis.conditions: Expose both the modified and unmodified alloys to high-temperature oxidation tests in synthetic air at temperatures between 700°C and 900°C for up to 48 hours.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 (alumina) layer on the alloy surface.
hypothesis.mechanism: Al2O3 has a Pilling–Bedworth ratio in the protective range (typically between 1 and 2) and forms a thermodynamically stable, slow-growing oxide. Increasing the Al content encourages its selective oxidation, which suppresses the diffusion of oxygen into the alloy and thereby reduces further oxidation. This contrasts with the less-protective mixed oxides (e.g., Mn- or Fe-based) that the baseline alloy forms.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The aluminum-doped HEA will show a lower mass gain per unit area, a thinner and more adherent oxide scale, and reduced oxide spallation relative to the baseline Cr-Mn-Fe-Co HEA. The improvement is expected to be moderate to significant, though the exact magnitude depends on the optimal Al level.
hypothesis.baseline: The unmodified equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co HEA, which forms a spinel-type mixed oxide layer prone to cracking and spallation at high temperatures.
hypothesis.boundary: Valid for high-temperature exposures in air within the 700°C to 900°C range; phase stability of the HEA must be maintained with the minor Al addition.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Exact quantitative gains in oxidation resistance and the optimal Al content require experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one of the baseline Cr-Mn-Fe-Co HEA and one with 3–5 at.% added Al. Expose both to 900°C in synthetic air for 48 hours. Characterize the oxide layers via XRD and SEM/EDS, measure mass gain, and assess adhesion properties.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area
Oxide scale thickness and phase composition via XRD
Adhesion and spallation extent via SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not exhibit a significantly lower mass gain and a more uniform, adherent Al2O3 scale relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C8

source_paper.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper's finding that ultrafine-grained microstructure in AlCoCrFeNi HEA leads to the formation of protective chromia and alumina layers, thereby reducing oxidation kinetics.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the paper’s mechanism by proposing an alternative severe plastic deformation route to maximize GB density and thereby further enhance the selective diffusion of protecting elements, which has not been explicitly tested in the original study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Enhancing grain-boundary mediated diffusion by further refining the microstructure will promote rapid, selective oxidation of Cr and Al to form a dense, protective Cr2O3/Al2O3 scale in high-entropy alloys at high temperatures.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy similar to AlCoCrFeNi in its as-cast or conventionally processed state with relatively coarse grains.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply an alternative severe plastic deformation process (e.g. equal-channel angular extrusion or high strain rate surface treatment) that drives the grain size further into the ultrafine regime (sub-micron scale), thus maximizing grain boundary density.
hypothesis.conditions: Conduct high temperature oxidation tests at 850–1050 °C for durations on the order of 100 h, comparing treatments.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Ultrafine grain structure with an increased fraction of grain boundaries (GBs) and higher surface free energy.
hypothesis.mechanism: A higher density of GBs acts as rapid diffusion paths for Cr and Al ions. This accelerated diffusion facilitates the timely formation of a continuous Cr2O3 top layer (which has a higher thermodynamic stability in a reactive environment) and a subsequent formation of an Al2O3 layer underneath, thereby suppressing the formation of nonprotective spinels and reducing further oxidation. This builds on selective oxidation theory as noted in the paper (e.g., PMC9026100::web::022).

In contrast, in microstructures with segregated Mn-rich regions, the formation of Mn oxides (which tend to be less adherent and more volatile) disrupts the continuity and adherence of the oxide layer. This mechanism underscores the critical role of microstructural homogeneity on the selective oxidation behavior in high-entropy alloys.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Homogenized CrFeCoNiMn alloys will show lower specific mass gain and feature continuous, Cr₂O₃-dominant oxide scales as observed by reduced porosity and minimal spallation, whereas heterogeneous alloys will display higher oxidation rates with discontinuous, Mn-rich oxide formations.
hypothesis.baseline: CrFeCoNiMn alloys with heterogeneous, multiphase microstructures that exhibit Mn-rich segregation.
hypothesis.boundary: Applicable for exposures above 900 °C in air or reactive gases, provided that processing can reliably produce either a single-phase or multiphase structure.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact quantitative oxidation protection provided by the Cr₂O₃ phase in this system is uncertain and could be influenced by the Cr/Mn ratio and alloy processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrFeCoNiMn samples: one processed to yield a homogeneous, single-phase structure and a second with a deliberately induced multiphase structure. Expose both sets to oxidation at >900 °C (e.g., 100 h) and perform controlled measurements.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area
SEM imaging of surface and cross-sectional oxide morphology
XRD analysis to identify Cr₂O₃ (versus Mn oxide) phases
EDS mapping for elemental distribution in the scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the single-phase alloy does not show a significantly more coherent, Cr-rich protective oxide layer with lower oxidation kinetics than the multiphase alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C8

source_paper.title: Precipitation behavior of AlxCoCrFeNi high entropy alloys under ion irradiation.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s findings on the importance of high configurational entropy and low atomic mobility in stabilizing phases are extended here by deliberately engineering the near-surface microstructure to control diffusion paths during high-temperature oxidation.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a specific laser surface modification step to tailor the near-surface microstructure—reducing grain boundary density and enhancing Cr uniformity—to promote formation and retention of a coherent protective oxide scale at temperatures above 900 °C, a mechanism not addressed in the original irradiation study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A laser surface remelting treatment that creates a homogenized, low–grain-boundary-density near‐surface region in single‐phase CrFeCoNiX alloys will promote formation of a coherent, protective Cr‐rich oxide scale upon exposure above 900 °C.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high‐entropy alloy in a conventionally cast single‐phase state with a typical fine-grained microstructure.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a pulsed laser surface remelting process to the as-cast alloy to produce an amorphous or ultrafine homogenized layer with significantly reduced grain boundary density and enhanced chemical uniformity (especially regarding critical oxidizing species such as Cr).
hypothesis.conditions: Subsequent prolonged exposure to oxidative or corrosive environments above 900 °C.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A near-surface region with fewer fast-diffusion pathways (i.e. grain boundaries) and a uniform elemental distribution, particularly in Cr, which is essential for forming protective oxides.
hypothesis.mechanism: Laser remelting induces rapid localized melting and re-solidification, resulting in a dense, homogenized layer that minimizes heterogeneity and grain-boundary networks. At high temperatures, the reduced diffusion pathways slow down excessive oxygen ingress and cation migration. This controlled oxidation allows selective formation of a thin, Cr-enriched oxide (e.g. Cr2O3) that is coherent and adherent because of the absence of disruptive microstructural defects. This leverages the known benefit of high configurational entropy in maintaining phase stability (as shown in PMC4999872::web::017::conclusions), while using surface microstructure control to tailor oxidation kinetics.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated alloys, laser-remelted samples are expected to develop a thinner, more uniform, and more adherent Cr-rich oxide scale with lower incidences of cracking or spallation.
hypothesis.baseline: CrFeCoNiX alloys produced by conventional casting and thermomechanical processing exhibiting typical fine-grained microstructures with abundant grain boundaries.
hypothesis.boundary: Applicable to single-phase high-entropy alloys exposed to oxidizing or corrosive conditions above 900 °C, where grain-boundary diffusion dominates oxidation kinetics.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The long-term thermal stability of the laser-treated near-surface region at extended high-temperature exposures and the exact kinetics of Cr segregation in the modified layer require further quantitative study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two identical batches of single-phase CrFeCoNiX samples. Subject one batch to pulsed laser surface remelting and leave the other untreated. Expose both sets to an oxidizing atmosphere at >900 °C for a predetermined duration. After exposure, perform cross-sectional TEM/SEM analysis, measure oxide scale thickness (via focused ion beam cross-sectioning), determine Cr concentration profiles (using XPS or AES), and assess oxide scale adhesion (via micro-scratch testing).
measurements: Grain size and grain boundary density (via EBSD/TEM)
Oxide thickness and morphology (via cross-sectional SEM/TEM)
Surface and sub-surface Cr enrichment (via XPS/AES depth profiling)
Adhesion quality (via micro-scratch or thermal cycling tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser-treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in oxide uniformity, coherence, and adhesion (e.g., comparable oxide thickness, irregular scale morphology, or high spallation rates similar to untreated samples), then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C9

source_paper.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s demonstration that protective alumina (and chromia) layers can form under favorable diffusion conditions in HEAs, extending that idea by showing that compositional enhancement (Al increase) plus mild grain refinement can overcome the limitations of the coarse-grained state.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis uniquely couples a modest Al content increase with a controlled, mild grain-refinement treatment—introducing additional surface diffusion pathways—to ensure sufficient Al delivery for forming a fault-tolerant, adherent alumina layer, which the paper did not explore.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A combined compositional and microstructural modification in CrFeCoNiAl HEAs – achieved by a modest increase in Al content together with a mild surface grain‐refinement treatment – will accelerate Al diffusion to the surface via enhanced grain boundary density, leading to the formation and persistence of a coherent, continuous alumina layer that resists cracking and spallation at temperatures above 900 °C.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiAl HEA in a conventional coarse-grained, as-cast state with baseline Al content.
hypothesis.intervention: Increase the Al content moderately (while avoiding brittle intermetallics) and perform a mild surface grain refinement treatment (e.g., short-duration, low-energy shot peening) that modestly increases the grain boundary density near the surface.
hypothesis.conditions: Exposure in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at >900 °C (e.g., 950 °C) for about 100 h.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A near-surface region with moderately refined grain structure providing additional fast diffusion paths for Al without inducing excessive internal oxidation.
hypothesis.mechanism: Mild grain refinement increases the density of grain boundaries, which act as rapid diffusion paths for Al. The increased Al supply, together with the high thermodynamic stability and favorable Pilling–Bedworth ratio of alumina, promotes the formation of a continuous, coherent Al2O3 layer. This protective scale is less prone to spallation because the enhanced grain boundary connectivity supports steady Al diffusion to heal minor defects that can develop during oxidation. This approach addresses the limitation of coarse-grained HEAs, which in the paper form mixed, nonprotective oxides due to insufficient elemental transport (PMC9026100::web::021).
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The modified HEA will exhibit a significantly lower cumulative mass gain (expected reduction of roughly 30–50% relative to the baseline coarse-grained alloy) and a densely adherent alumina-dominated scale that shows minimal cracking or spallation after prolonged high-temperature exposure.
hypothesis.baseline: CrFeCoNiAl HEA with standard (lower) Al content and a coarse-grained microstructure, which tends to form unstable, mixed oxide layers with spinel phases (PMC9026100::web::021).
hypothesis.boundary: The effect is expected to be operative when the Al increase is kept within the solubility limits of the HEA, and the mild refinement technique is optimized to enhance surface grain boundary density without inducing deep internal oxidation or phase destabilization. It is applicable for single- or multiphase solid-solution HEAs exposed to temperatures above 900 °C for durations around 100 h.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact quantitative impact of the combined adjustments on oxide scale thickness and mass gain reduction is uncertain, and an excessively aggressive grain refinement may lead to increased internal oxidation; careful calibration is necessary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrFeCoNiAl HEA samples: one set with modestly increased Al content combined with a mild shot peening treatment (to produce slight grain refinement) and one set as untreated baseline. Expose both sets to oxidation at 950 °C for 100 h in an oxidative/corrosive atmosphere. Use SEM/EDS and XRD to assess oxide scale composition, continuity, and morphology, and record cumulative mass gain.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area
Oxide phase identification and continuity (via XRD and SEM/EDS)
Grain size distribution near the surface (to confirm refinement)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated HEA does not form a predominantly continuous, coherent alumina scale and does not exhibit a significantly lower mass gain (within the expected ~30–50% improvement) compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C10

source_paper.title: High-Temperature Wear Behaviour of Spark Plasma Sintered AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 High-Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s demonstration of high-temperature oxide formation and known principles of spinel-based passivation in oxidation resistance, combined with strategies to modify oxide compositions via controlled pre-oxidation.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis converts the traditionally deleterious oxidation behavior of Mn by intentionally forming a mixed (Cr,Mn) spinel interlayer through controlled pre-oxidation—a novel approach not explored in the paper—to achieve a protective, graded duplex oxide scale.

hypothesis.hypothesis: In SPS‐processed CrFeCoNiMn alloys, a controlled pre-oxidation treatment in a carefully adjusted oxygen potential can trigger the in situ formation of a mixed (Cr,Mn) spinel interlayer that transforms the typically non-protective Mn oxidation into a coherent, graded duplex oxide scale at temperatures above 900 °C.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiMn alloy produced by SPS featuring a fine, single- or multiphase solid-solution microstructure where Mn is uniformly distributed but prone to forming porous, non-adherent Mn oxides upon direct oxidation.
hypothesis.intervention: Subject the alloy surface to a brief, low-temperature pre-oxidation (e.g., 700 °C for 30 minutes) in a controlled atmosphere with a moderately low oxygen partial pressure to promote the preferential formation of a thin, mixed (Cr,Mn) spinel interlayer.
hypothesis.conditions: Follow this with exposure to an oxidizing or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C under typical service conditions.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A deliberately engineered thin (Cr,Mn) spinel interlayer that acts as a compliant bonding agent between the metallic substrate and the overlying high-temperature oxide scale.
hypothesis.mechanism: Under carefully controlled pre-oxidation conditions, limited oxidation occurs such that Mn’s tendency for porous oxide formation is mitigated through its reaction with Cr already present in the alloy. This results in a thin (Cr,Mn) spinel with a higher effective Pilling–Bedworth ratio than pure Mn oxide. Upon subsequent high-temperature exposure, this interlayer promotes the growth of a duplex, graded oxide scale that accommodates thermal stresses and minimizes crack propagation and spallation.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Relative to standard SPS CrFeCoNiMn alloys (without pre-oxidation), the treated specimens will form a stable, duplex oxide scale with improved adhesion, evidenced by reduced oxidation weight gain and enhanced resistance to thermal cycling.
hypothesis.baseline: CrFeCoNiMn alloys processed by SPS and directly exposed to high-temperature conditions without the tailored pre-oxidation step, which typically develop discontinuous and spall-prone Mn-rich oxides.
hypothesis.boundary: The approach is applicable for oxidation conditions above 900 °C; careful calibration of oxygen partial pressure during pre-oxidation is critical to avoid the formation of excessively thick or brittle oxide layers.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The optimal oxygen potential and time required to reliably form the (Cr,Mn) spinel interlayer, as well as its long-term stability under cyclic thermal conditions, need to be empirically determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of SPS-processed CrFeCoNiMn alloy samples: one set receiving the controlled low-temperature pre-oxidation treatment and one set kept as-sintered. Expose both sets to an oxidizing atmosphere at >900 °C for a fixed period.
measurements: SEM/EDS and TEM to characterize the presence, thickness, and continuity of the (Cr,Mn) spinel interlayer and the overall duplex oxide structure.
XRD and Raman spectroscopy to differentiate oxide phases and confirm the formation of the mixed spinel.
Oxidation weight gain measurements.
Adhesion and thermal cycling tests (e.g., scratch and spallation tests) to gauge the mechanical integrity of the oxide scale.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with pre-oxidation do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in duplex oxide coherence, adhesion, and reduced weight gain compared to the untreated controls, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C3

source_paper.title: Thermodynamic Insights into the Oxidation Mechanisms of CrMnFeCoNi High-Entropy Alloy Using In Situ X-ray Diffraction.

hypotheses.builds_on: the established mechanism that alumina scales are more protective due to their favorable thermodynamics and adherence properties, as seen in alumina-forming stainless steels (see TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::011).
hypotheses.what_is_new: It introduces a compositional and processing change specifically in CrFeCoNiAl HEAs to intentionally form a dual-layer structure with an inner, stable alumina barrier, shifting from the generally observed unstable multiphase oxide formation.

hypothesis.hypothesis: In a CrFeCoNiAl high-entropy alloy, elevating the aluminum content and/or promoting its surface enrichment via pre-oxidation treatments will induce the formation of an inner layer of Al₂O₃ that acts as a coherent diffusion barrier beneath any transient outer oxides, thus stabilizing the overall oxide scale during exposure above 900 °C.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A multiphase or single-phase CrFeCoNiAl alloy with a baseline aluminum level previously showing mixed oxide behavior.
hypothesis.intervention: Modify the alloy composition to increase the Al content (or use surface pre-treatments that promote Al segregation to the surface) to encourage early formation of an Al₂O₃ sublayer.
hypothesis.conditions: Exposure in an oxidative/corrosive atmosphere above 900 °C. The treatment should be applied so that the alloy is either in the designed single-phase or controlled multiphase state.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A coherent, stable, and low-growth-rate Al₂O₃ inner layer at the metal-oxide interface that bonds well with both the substrate and any outer, less protective oxides.
hypothesis.mechanism: Aluminum has a high affinity for oxygen and forms Al₂O₃, which is known to exhibit a favorable Pilling–Bedworth ratio (typically above unity, as described in TXT::wikipedia::Chromium::005 and TXT::wikipedia::Passivation_(chemistry)::004). The formation of an early, continuous Al₂O₃ layer reduces oxygen diffusion into the substrate and minimizes thermal mismatch stresses, thereby preventing the development of unstable, cracking Mn-rich or mixed oxides.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The Al-enhanced alloy will display a two-layer oxide structure with a coherent, thin Al₂O₃ foundation that persists through high-temperature exposures, leading to reduced spallation and improved oxidation resistance relative to the baseline alloy.
hypothesis.baseline: A CrFeCoNiAl alloy with lower Al content that tends to form thicker, multiphase oxide scales with poorer adhesion (e.g., Mn2O3 and Mn₃O₄ mixed scales observed in PMC10384371::web::019::3_3_htxrd_in_air).
hypothesis.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for high-temperature (>900 °C) exposure in oxidative atmospheres; however, it requires that the alloy remains in a solid-solution state and does not form deleterious intermetallic phases due to excessive Al.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise Al content required to form a pure and coherent Al₂O₃ sublayer while maintaining the overall alloy integrity is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CrFeCoNiAl alloy samples with the baseline Al content and with increased Al content (or use a surface enrichment pre-treatment). Oxidize the samples at >900 °C in air. Post-exposure, perform cross-sectional analysis (SEM/EDS) and XRD to assess the oxide layering and adhesion.
measurements: Identification of an Al₂O₃ phase at the metal-oxide interface (XRD)
Layer thickness and continuity via cross-sectional SEM
Adhesion quality tests (e.g., thermal cycling or mechanical scratch tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the increased-Al samples do not exhibit a coherent, continuous Al₂O₃ sublayer with improved adhesion and reduced spallation compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is invalidated.

expert_context.question: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

hypotheses.label: C2

source_paper.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s detailed investigation of oxidation-driven compositional inversion and element-specific diffusion (as shown by APT and XANES) and uses the idea of controlled pre-oxidation to manipulate surface chemistry as a means to stabilize the oxide layer.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a sequential oxidation treatment—first tailoring surface composition by a controlled pre‐oxidation step and then carrying out full oxidation—to achieve a graded, protective oxide layer, a strategy that has not been explored in the original work.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Controlled Pre‐Oxidation to Tailor Surface Composition and Establish a Protective Nucleation Template
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A single‐phase CrFeCoNiX alloy (with X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a homogeneous, well-sintered FCC state prepared by conventional melting, homogenization, and recrystallization, with a mirror-polished surface.
hypothesis.intervention: Subject the alloy surface to a controlled pre‐oxidation treatment in a mildly reducing or weakly oxidizing atmosphere at an intermediate temperature (≈850 °C) before exposing the alloy to a full oxidative/corrosive environment above 900 °C.
hypothesis.conditions: A two-step thermal treatment: initial pre‐oxidation at approximately 850 °C in a controlled atmosphere (e.g., low oxygen partial pressure or slightly reducing) followed by exposure at >900 °C in an oxidative/corrosive atmosphere.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: An engineered gradient layer at the surface wherein faster-diffusing elements are partially depleted and slower-oxidizing, passivating elements (such as Cr and Al or Si) are enriched, thereby forming an optimal nucleation template for the subsequent formation of a coherent protective oxide.
hypothesis.mechanism: During the pre-oxidation step under controlled atmospheres, faster diffusing species (e.g., Mn) are preferentially removed from the extreme surface, leading to an enrichment of elements like Cr and Al (or Si) that form slower-growing, more adherent oxides. This tailored surface composition then acts as an ideal template during the subsequent exposure at >900 °C, promoting the nucleation and growth of a coherent, slow-growing oxide layer with improved structural integrity. The graded compositional transition reduces the thermal expansion mismatch and stress accumulation that can lead to spallation.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The alloy samples that undergo the controlled pre‐oxidation treatment will develop a graded, coherent oxide scale with reduced thickness and improved adhesion (i.e., less cracking or spallation) compared to samples that are directly oxidized at >900 °C without the pre-treatment.
hypothesis.baseline: Identical CrFeCoNiX alloy samples subjected directly to oxidation at >900 °C without any pre‐oxidation step.
hypothesis.boundary: The pre‐oxidation treatment must be carefully optimized for temperature, duration, and atmosphere. Excessively aggressive pre‐oxidation might lead to a porous or excessively depleted surface, while insufficient treatment may not yield the desired compositional gradient.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The optimal pre‐oxidation conditions (temperature, time, atmosphere) that result in the desired surface enrichment and how robust the templated layer is during subsequent high-temperature exposure remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples: one subjected to a controlled pre‐oxidation treatment at ≈850 °C under a mildly reducing/low-oxygen atmosphere followed by full oxidation at >900 °C, and another set directly oxidized at >900 °C. Analyze the oxide layers using cross-sectional TEM, APT, and XPS to assess the oxide’s thickness, composition gradient, and structural coherence. Perform thermal cycling tests to check for spallation.
measurements: Surface compositional profiles and oxide layer structure (via TEM and APT)
Oxide phase composition (using XPS and XRD)
Mechanical integrity through thermal cycling and SEM imaging of surface cracks/spallation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples undergoing pre‐oxidation do not exhibit a significantly more graded and coherent oxide layer with reduced cracking/spallation compared to the as-oxidized samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C12

source_paper.title: The Effect of Copper on the Microstructure, Wear and Corrosion Resistance of CoCrCuFeNi High-Entropy Alloys Manufactured by Powder Metallurgy.

hypotheses.builds_on: This builds on the general understanding of oxidation in HEAs and passivation behavior (as described in the background texts on passivation and the Pilling–Bedworth ratio) and extends it by using controlled, low-level silicon doping to tailor the oxide scale composition.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis specifically tests a silicon substitution strategy at a lower doping level (≈3 at.%) that minimizes silicide formation while promoting an amorphous SiO2 phase within a Cr2O3 matrix, a mechanism not explored in the original copper-doping study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Reducing the silicon doping level in CrFeCoNi from 0 to about 3 at.% will promote the in situ formation of a nanoscale, amorphous SiO2 component that intermixes with the protective Cr2O3 scale, thereby enhancing strain accommodation and adhesion at temperatures above 900 °C.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) in a single-phase solid-solution state with no silicon.
hypothesis.intervention: Substitute about 3 at.% of one of the base elements (e.g., partial replacement of Ni) with silicon to form CrFeCoNiSi (≈3 at.% Si).
hypothesis.conditions: Exposure to a high-temperature oxidative or corrosive atmosphere (e.g., oxygen-rich gas with trace water vapor) at temperatures above 900 °C under cyclic thermal loading.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A composite oxide scale in which a thin, amorphous, dispersed SiO2 phase is embedded in and at the metal/oxide interface with a continuous Cr2O3 layer.
hypothesis.mechanism: Thermodynamic calculations and CALPHAD assessments (from established literature on oxidation and passivation [TXT::wikipedia::Passivation_(chemistry)::004, TXT::wikipedia::Pilling–Bedworth_ratio::001]) indicate that at low (<3 at.%) silicon levels, the alloy remains in a solid solution without triggering silicide formation. At high temperature, silicon has a high oxygen affinity and oxidizes preferentially to form an amorphous silica phase that mixes with Cr2O3. The amorphous SiO2 phase can accommodate thermal expansion mismatches and deflect cracking, thereby reducing spallation of the oxide scale.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The Si-doped CrFeCoNiSi alloy will form a thinner, more adherent, and crack-resistant composite oxide scale with lower spallation rates compared to the undoped CrFeCoNi alloy. The improvement is expected to be significant (qualitatively >30–50% reduction in defect density) though the precise magnitude requires experimental quantification.
hypothesis.baseline: Undoped CrFeCoNi HEA tested under the same high-temperature oxidative or corrosive conditions.
hypothesis.boundary: Temperature ≥900 °C in oxidizing atmospheres typical of high-temperature industrial or aerospace environments, with cyclic thermal stresses applied.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact volume fraction and distribution of the amorphous SiO2 phase and its effect on overall mechanical compliance is uncertain and needs experimental validation; thermodynamic predictions support the mechanism at ~3 at.% silicon but detailed kinetics remain to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples via identical processing routes: one set of undoped CrFeCoNi and one set with 3 at.% Si substitution (CrFeCoNiSi). Subject both sets to cyclic oxidation treatments at ~950 °C in a controlled oxygen-rich atmosphere. Perform cross-sectional analysis using TEM/SEM combined with EDS and XRD to evaluate oxide scale thickness, phase distribution, and crack density. Additionally, conduct thermal shock tests to assess spallation.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and morphology (via TEM/SEM)
Phase identification and distribution (using XRD and EDS)
Crack density and spallation incidence (thermal shock and adhesion tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Si-doped alloy shows no statistically significant improvement in oxide scale uniformity, adhesion, and reduction of cracking/spallation compared to the undoped alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C3

source_paper.title: High Temperature Oxidation Behavior of an Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co High-Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s findings of oxide instability driven by excessive Mn oxidation and uncontrolled diffusion (PMC8346963, sections 3.1–3.2) and on diffusion-based segregation principles in alloy systems.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a specific, two-step thermal treatment to induce controlled nanoscale Cr enrichment and thus form a graded, dual-layer oxide structure with improved adhesion—a novel approach not previously reported in the original work.

hypothesis.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiMn high-entropy alloys, a tailored two-step thermal treatment can induce controlled nanoscale Cr enrichment at grain boundaries, thereby promoting the in situ formation of an adherent Cr2O3 sublayer beneath a modified Mn-rich oxide and mitigating the spallation observed at temperatures above 900 °C.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A homogenous, single-phase CrFeCoNiMn HEA with a uniformly distributed FCC structure produced by conventional processing.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a two-step heat treatment: first, a short-duration low-temperature annealing (e.g., around 800 °C) to initiate slight Cr segregation toward grain boundaries without full phase separation, followed by a rapid ramp to the oxidation temperature (≥900 °C).
hypothesis.conditions: Oxidation in synthetic air (or corrosive atmosphere) at temperatures ≥900 °C for durations from 12 to 48 h.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A graded oxide scale consisting of a continuous, adherent Cr2O3 sublayer (formed at Cr-enriched grain boundaries) that mechanically anchors an outer Mn-rich oxide layer.
hypothesis.mechanism: The controlled two-step thermal treatment exploits the differential diffusion rates of Cr and Mn. The initial low-temperature step induces mild Cr enrichment at grain boundaries without triggering full phase separation. Once the oxidation temperature is reached, the Cr-enriched regions preferentially form a stable Cr2O3 sublayer (which possesses a high Pilling–Bedworth ratio and good mechanical integrity). This sublayer acts as a robust diffusion barrier and mechanical anchor that mitigates the spallation typically observed from Mn-rich, less-adherent oxide formation. The resulting graded oxide scale exhibits improved resistance to cracking and delamination.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared with a baseline CrFeCoNiMn alloy processed without the two-step treatment, the treated sample will form a dual-layer oxide scale with a continuous, well-adherent Cr2O3 sublayer (documented via cross-sectional SEM/TEM and EDS mapping), reduced overall mass gain, and fewer spallation events under thermal cycling.
hypothesis.baseline: A conventionally processed homogenous CrFeCoNiMn alloy that develops unstable, spalling mixed Mn-rich oxides upon high-temperature exposure as reported in PMC8346963.
hypothesis.boundary: Applicable to equiatomic CrFeCoNiMn HEAs where the two-step thermal treatment can be applied without triggering detrimental phase separation, with oxidation tests performed at ≥900 °C in synthetic air for 12–48 h.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The feasibility and reproducibility of inducing controlled nanoscale Cr segregation without unwanted phase separation require further experimental optimization; precise gradient parameters (e.g., temperature differential and annealing duration) may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrFeCoNiMn samples: one subjected to the tailored two-step thermal treatment (low-temperature anneal followed by rapid ramp-up to ≥900 °C) and one maintained as a homogeneous control. Expose both sets to oxidation at 900 °C for 48 h.
measurements: TEM/SEM with EDS mapping to detect nanoscale Cr enrichment and verify the presence of a continuous Cr2O3 sublayer
Mass gain and oxidation kinetics measurements
Adhesion tests (e.g., thermal cycling or scratch tests) to assess the mechanical integrity of the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally treated sample does not display a graded oxide scale with a continuous Cr2O3 sublayer and does not show a significant improvement in oxidation resistance and reduced spallation compared to the homogeneous control, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C6

source_paper.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: the general idea from superalloy technology where controlled additions (like Al and Si) aid in forming protective oxide or silicate layers for improved high-temperature performance.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This proposal introduces the concept of tailoring Si content specifically in CrFeCoNi-based HEAs to engineer an interfacial silicate layer, a strategy not previously explored in such alloys for high-temperature oxidation resistance.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Controlled Si addition in CrFeCoNiSi alloys promotes the in-situ formation of a silicate-rich interfacial sublayer that anchors the protective oxide, reducing thermal mismatch and hindering spallation above 900 °C.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiSi high-entropy alloy produced with coarse grains typical of as-cast conditions.
hypothesis.intervention: Tailor the alloy composition by incorporating a controlled amount of Si, followed by a pre-oxidation heat treatment designed to induce Si segregation to the oxide-metal interface.
hypothesis.conditions: Expose the alloy to an oxidative environment at temperatures above 900 °C, for exposure durations consistent with service conditions (e.g., 100 h).
hypothesis.structural_mediator: An interfacial silicate (or silica/silicate) layer at the oxide–metal boundary that reduces interfacial strain and serves as a chemical barrier against further oxygen ingress.
hypothesis.mechanism: Silicon has a strong affinity for oxygen and, upon heat treatment, segregates preferentially to grain boundaries and surface regions. There, it reacts to form a thin, thermodynamically stable silicate sublayer. This sublayer minimizes thermal expansion mismatch between the metallic substrate and the growing oxide, enhancing adhesion and retarding further oxygen diffusion to maintain a slow-growing, coherent protective oxide scale.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to a Si-free baseline, the Si-containing alloy will develop an additional silicate sublayer, exhibiting reduced oxidation kinetics and improved scale adhesion. hypothesis.conditions: High-temperature exposure above 900 °C in an atmosphere with carefully controlled oxygen and water vapor levels; the ion implantation dose and energy are optimized to avoid excessive damage while enhancing surface Si concentration.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A nanostructured, Si-enriched surface layer with an increased density of defects and grain boundaries that promotes rapid and selective oxidation of Si to form an amorphous silica film.
hypothesis.mechanism: The ion implantation process creates a supersaturated Si surface region that, upon rapid high-temperature oxidation, oxidizes preferentially to form SiO2. The high defect density in the implanted layer (and the presence of water vapor) favors the formation of an amorphous rather than crystalline silica scale. This amorphous scale, owing to its more uniform thermal expansion and lower internal stresses, remains adherent and cracks less readily during thermal cycling.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: After 100 hours at ~950 °C, TEM and XPS will reveal an amorphous SiO2 scale, less than 100 nm in thickness, with lower oxidation weight gain and better adhesion compared to non-implanted controls.
hypothesis.baseline: CrFeCoNiSi HEA samples processed without ion implantation, where oxidation leads to thicker, more crystalline (and likely noncoherent) oxide scales with higher susceptibility to cracking or spallation.
hypothesis.boundary: Applicable to CrFeCoNiSi HEAs in which surface modification by ion implantation is feasible, under exposure conditions above 900 °C with precisely regulated oxygen and water vapor levels.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The detailed oxidation kinetics of the ion–implanted Si layer at high temperatures remain to be established; there is uncertainty regarding the threshold implantation dose required to reliably achieve an amorphous silica barrier.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CrFeCoNiSi HEA samples with and without Si ion implantation. Expose both groups to 950 °C in a controlled humid oxidation atmosphere for 100 hours. Characterize the surface oxide using TEM (to assess thickness and amorphous/crystalline nature), XPS (to confirm chemical state), and measure oxidation weight gains.
measurements: TEM cross-sections with selected area electron diffraction (SAED) for amorphous characterization
XPS spectroscopy for chemical composition and bonding state
Gravimetric oxidation weight gain analysis
Nano-scratch adhesion tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ion–implanted samples do not demonstrate a significantly thinner, predominantly amorphous, and more adherent silica layer compared to the non-implanted controls, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C9

source_paper.title: An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s discussion of how heterogeneous oxidation behavior due to different phase compositions (e.g., dendritic versus interdendritic regions) leads to defect formation in the oxide scale (PMC6513993::web::004::oxidation_behaviour_at_1000_c and related sections).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis shifts focus from elemental composition modifications to processing route adjustments to homogenize the microstructure, thereby targeting stress minimization at the oxide/substrate interface—a condition not explored in the referenced study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Uniform oxide scale formation in CrFeCoNiMn can be achieved by tailoring the microstructure through a post-casting thermomechanical processing step, which minimizes compositional heterogeneities that lead to localized stress and subsequent oxide cracking or spallation.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiMn high-entropy alloy as-cast, likely containing microstructural heterogeneities (e.g., dendritic and interdendritic regions) that result in non-uniform oxidation.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a thermomechanical homogenization treatment (e.g., hot working followed by a high-temperature anneal) to refine the grain structure and achieve a more homogeneous solid solution.
hypothesis.conditions: High-temperature oxidation testing above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere over long exposures (e.g., 100–200 hours).
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A uniform, equiaxed microstructure with reduced segregation leads to the formation of a more continuously adherent and coherent oxide layer on the consistently composed substrate.
hypothesis.mechanism: The hypothesis is based on the idea that microstructural heterogeneities, such as dendrite/interdendrite variations, lead to locally varying oxidation kinetics (as observed in the paper for NV1, PMC6513993::web::003::pre_oxidation_microstructure), which in turn produce internal stresses and defects in the oxide scale. By homogenizing the microstructure, diffusion pathways and oxidation rates become more uniform, promoting the nucleation and lateral growth of a continuous oxide layer that better accommodates thermal stresses.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: An oxidized sample with a uniform, dense, and slow-growing protective oxide layer that exhibits significantly reduced cracking or spallation compared to the as-cast, heterogeneous structure.
hypothesis.baseline: The as-cast CrFeCoNiMn alloy with pronounced dendritic structures that has been shown to form unstable oxide scales prone to localized defect formation and eventual spallation.
hypothesis.boundary: High-temperature oxidation conditions (above 900 °C) for durations up to 200 hours in controlled atmospheres.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While processing effects on oxide coherence are supported in other alloy systems, the direct quantitative impact of microstructural homogenization on oxidation kinetics in CrFeCoNiMn HEAs specifically has limited prior evidence.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two samples of CrFeCoNiMn: one as-cast and one processed via thermomechanical homogenization. Subject both to oxidation at 950 °C in an oxidative atmosphere for 200 hours.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (SEM/EDS, XRD) of the oxide scale and the underlying microstructure
Mass gain measurements and spallation testing
Measurement of oxide layer continuity and defect density
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the homogenized sample does not exhibit a clearly more uniform oxide layer (with lower defect density and improved adhesion) and reduced oxidation kinetics compared to the as-cast sample, the hypothesis will be falsified.
